children.text: In the stated model a star illuminates a primary mirror of area \(A_m=25\,\mathrm{m^2}\), effective focal length \(f=130\,\mathrm m\), focusing onto a CCD. A red giant at distance 89 light-years has temperature 3600 K and diameter \(d_o=1.7\times10^{11}\,\mathrm m\). Use \(\lambda=800\,\mathrm{nm}\), \(c=2.998\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(k_B=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}\), \(\sigma=5.670374419\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W/(m^2K^4)}\), and 365 days per year. Dark current is \(i_d=i_0e^{-|\Delta E_g|/(6k_BT)}\), measured as electrons per second. The detector-count graph is retained below. Part C uses five parallel, thin, square sunshield sheets, each 200 square metres, separated by 25 cm at the perimeter, with small emissivity epsilon on both faces and diffuse reflections. Net intersheet exchange is \(\alpha Q_{ij}\), gap loss is \(\beta Q_{ij}\), with \(Q_{ij}=\epsilon\sigma A_s(T_i^4-T_j^4)\), following the stipulated approximate difference-flux convention. Space background is negligible. Part D studies adiabatic steady helium throttling through a porous plug from states 1 to 2, with negligible change in bulk kinetic energy. Helium is not ideal and stays gaseous.

statement.text:
James Webb Space Telescope
In the stated model a star illuminates a primary mirror of area \(A_m=25\,\mathrm{m^2}\), effective focal length \(f=130\,\mathrm m\), focusing onto a CCD. A red giant at distance 89 light-years has temperature 3600 K and diameter \(d_o=1.7\times10^{11}\,\mathrm m\). Use \(\lambda=800\,\mathrm{nm}\), \(c=2.998\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(k_B=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}\), \(\sigma=5.670374419\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W/(m^2K^4)}\), and 365 days per year. Dark current is \(i_d=i_0e^{-|\Delta E_g|/(6k_BT)}\), measured as electrons per second. The detector-count graph is retained below. Part C uses five parallel, thin, square sunshield sheets, each 200 square metres, separated by 25 cm at the perimeter, with small emissivity epsilon on both faces and diffuse reflections. Net intersheet exchange is \(\alpha Q_{ij}\), gap loss is \(\beta Q_{ij}\), with \(Q_{ij}=\epsilon\sigma A_s(T_i^4-T_j^4)\), following the stipulated approximate difference-flux convention. Space background is negligible. Part D studies adiabatic steady helium throttling through a porous plug from states 1 to 2, with negligible change in bulk kinetic energy. Helium is not ideal and stays gaseous.
A.1. Geometrical image size
Calculate the focused geometrical image diameter.
A.2. Diffraction spot
Estimate the diameter of the central diffraction maximum.
A.3. Uncooled detector temperature
If the black detector can radiate only from its top imaging surface, find equilibrium temperature at the stellar image, with formula and estimate.
B.1. Thermal threshold scale

Use the dark-current plot to estimate the temperature scale of thermal photons capable of exciting a detector electron.
B.2. Count uncertainty
For readout uncertainty \(\sigma_r\), dark current id, photon rate p and exposure tau, find total uncertainty.
B.3. Ten-sigma photon rate
Use detector temperature 7.5 K, exposure \(10^4\,\mathrm s\) and read noise 14. Find minimum photon rate such that its count equals ten times total uncertainty.
B.4. Incident photon intensity
Take photon energy just equal to the inferred gap. Find irradiance on the primary mirror.
C.1. Five-sheet temperatures

Derive first- and fifth-sheet equilibrium temperatures in terms of incident solar intensity I0, alpha and beta.
C.2. Geometrical exchange estimates

For epsilon=0.05, estimate alpha and beta using the gap as a black absorbing perimeter.
C.3. Numerical shield temperatures
Use \(I_0=1360\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\) and your estimates to find T1 and T5.
D.1. Throttling comparisons

For one mole compare state 1 versus 2 for internal energy U, temperature T, entropy S, pressure P and volume V. Use greater, less, equal or undetermined. Both pipes have equal cross section and downstream bulk speed is slightly greater.
D.2. Conserved throttling quantity
Find the conserved combination of U,P,V and derive it.
D.3. Helium enthalpy graph

For specific volume \(V_2=0.100\,\mathrm{m^3/kg}\) and T2=7.5 K, use the original helium U-V graph to determine specific enthalpy. Solid curves are isentropes, dashed curves isotherms. Show the construction.
D.4. Maximum inlet temperature
Use the same graph to find the highest possible inlet temperature consistent with the conserved enthalpy.
D.5. Inlet pressure
For the maximum inlet temperature find P1 from the graph.

children.text: The small angular size is \(d_o/D\). Thus \(d_i=fd_o/D=26.2\,\mu\mathrm m\).

Use an equal-area circular aperture \(D_m=2\sqrt{A_m/\pi}=5.64\,\mathrm m\). The Airy diameter is \(d_d=2.44\lambda f/D_m=45.0\,\mu\mathrm m\). This is the equal-area circular-aperture Airy estimate. The simpler diameter \(2\lambda f/D_m\) is 36.9 micrometres. The actual segmented aperture has a different diffraction pattern. State the aperture and diameter convention, then compare the estimate in self-review.

The collected power is \(P=A_m\sigma T_*^4(d_o/(2D))^2\). If it is uniformly deposited over spot diameter d, balance \(P=\sigma T_i^4\pi d^2/4\): \[T_i=T_*\left(\frac{A_md_o^2}{\pi D^2d^2}\right)^{1/4}.\] With geometrical d=di this is about 530 K. Taking the source approximate broadened diameter d=di+dd gives about 320 K. A diffraction-only area gives about 410 K. State the spot model. A real point-spread function has nonuniform intensity, so these are effective spot temperatures.

The graph slope of log base 10 current against 1/T is approximately -100 K. Hence \(|\Delta E_g|/(6k_B)\simeq100\ln10=230\,\mathrm K\), and the characteristic photon thermal-energy scale is \(|\Delta E_g|/k_B\simeq1380\,\mathrm K\), of order \(10^3\,\mathrm K\). A thermal spectrum has no sharp cutoff, so the intended answer is a scale.

Read id approximately 5 electrons/s from the graph. Put P=p tau. Solve \(P^2=100(14^2+5\times10^4+P)\), obtaining P approximately 2291 and \(p=0.229\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Graph-reading uncertainty gives roughly 0.206 to 0.250 per second.
The threshold photon energy is about \(1380k_B=1.91\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm J\). Thus \(I=p\Delta E_g/A_m\simeq1.75\times10^{-22}\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\).

Let \(q_i=\epsilon\sigma A_sT_i^4\), \(f_i=\alpha(q_i-q_{i+1})\), and \(r=1+\beta/\alpha\). The source recurrence is \(f_{i-1}=rf_i\), with \(f_4=q_5\). Summing differences gives \(q_1=Kq_5\), \[K=1+(1+r+r^2+r^3)/\alpha.\] Sheet-one balance is \(\epsilon A_sI_0=q_1+rf_1=(K+r^4)q_5\). Hence \[T_5=\left[\frac{I_0}{\sigma(K+r^4)}\right]^{1/4},\quad T_1=\left[\frac{I_0K}{\sigma(K+r^4)}\right]^{1/4}.\] This explicitly follows the stipulated difference-flux recurrence. A physical view-factor model for gap radiation instead depends on a sum of surface emissions. The official discussion acknowledges that distinction, so do not combine the two models silently.

The gap area is \(A_g=4h\sqrt{A_s}=14.14\,\mathrm{m^2}\). Repeated diffuse reflection weights the two sheet absorbing areas epsilon As and the open gap. Therefore \(\alpha\simeq\epsilon A_s/(2\epsilon A_s+A_g)=0.293\), while the escape probability is \(\beta_{\mathrm{prime}}\simeq A_g/(2\epsilon A_s+A_g)=0.414\). This is a probability for total radiation, not automatically the beta multiplying a temperature difference. Using beta approximately beta prime is the elementary problem approximation. A conversion requires temperature ratios and gives a somewhat larger effective beta.

Using the explicit C.1 recurrence with alpha=0.293 and beta=0.414 gives r=2.414, K=80.60 and \(T_1\simeq360\,\mathrm K,T_5\simeq120\,\mathrm K\). Different self-consistent gap approximations change the estimates. The retained official solution tabulates roughly 380 K and 102 K for rounded alpha=0.3,beta=0.4, but this does not follow the displayed recurrence used here. Formula and convention consistency matter, so this is self-review.

Pressure decreases, entropy increases through irreversibility, and equal-area mass continuity with higher downstream speed implies molar volume increases. Thus P1>P2, S1<S2, V1<V2. For an unspecified real gas the signs of T2-T1 and U2-U1 are not determined by these facts alone. The official key asserts U1<U2 from viscous dissipation, but this neglects the competing pressure-work terms. From conserved enthalpy, U2-U1=P1V1-P2V2, whose sign needs an equation of state.

Upstream gas does work P1V1 on a mole entering the plug, while that mole does P2V2 on downstream gas. No heat is exchanged and kinetic energy changes are negligible, so \(U_2-U_1=P_1V_1-P_2V_2\). Thus \(H=U+PV\) is constant. More precisely steady flow conserves specific enthalpy plus bulk kinetic energy per mass.

At the specified point draw the local isentrope tangent. Since \((\partial U/\partial V)_S=-P\), its intercept at V=0 is U+PV. Bracket with nearby tangents and interpolate: approximately \(40.7\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}\). The additional official answer-sheet graph and full solution are supplied because the archive retained solution ends before Part D.

From the enthalpy intercept draw candidate tangents to isentropes. Their contact points trace states of the same enthalpy. The largest isotherm touched is approximately 11 K. Above that inlet temperature no state on the required enthalpy locus reaches the specified outlet.
Pressure is minus the isentrope tangent slope. With the constructed inlet point, the graph gives approximately \(1.8\,\mathrm{MPa}\), with rough graphical estimates around 1.6 to 2.4 MPa.
